findings.quote: Each worker is held by a client-side limiter to at most 5 requests in any one-second window.
Nobody has checked whether the capture endpoint collapses repeats that share an idempotency key into one capture, and the payments team has not confirmed it either.
In writing, the provider has stated that the limits on our account are 20 requests per second and 1,000,000 requests per day.
From release 4.9 onward, customer emails are written by a single code path that first locks the tenant row and rejects an email already held by that tenant, so no duplicate pair has appeared since.
The limits that actually apply to our account have not been confirmed with the provider, and the plan has no figure for them.
Whether the capture endpoint treats repeated requests with the same idempotency key as a single capture has not been checked, and the payments team has not confirmed it.
'Internal Root 2023' is dropped from the trust bundle on day 5, at which point its private key, held offline from day 1 onward, is destroyed.
Nobody has timed the rollback job against a copy of the database at production size, so the duration of the down-migration and redeploy at 400 GB is not known.
Under INFO, the logger adds each request header's name and value, substituting the string '[redacted]' for the values of Cookie and X-Api-Key.
For the idempotency key the worker generates a brand-new random UUID on each attempt, retries included.
Base backups and archived WAL are both retained for 7 days, and a nightly lifecycle job deletes anything older.
The job reads the closed month-end snapshot, which no longer changes once the month is closed, and sends it in batches of 500 records.
Since release 4.9, the only code path that writes customer emails locks the tenant row first and refuses an email the tenant already has, so no duplicate pairs have been created since then.
It then builds customers_tenant_email_uq with CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY and attaches it to the table as the constraint once the build finishes.
Requests carrying an idempotency key the processor has seen in the last 24 hours get the original result back with no second charge, whereas any key it has not seen produces a fresh charge.
A client-side limiter in each worker caps it at 5 requests in any one-second window.

Under the release policy, a release declared failed has to be completely rolled back within 15 minutes, since the outage clock in the contract with our largest merchant runs until the prior version is serving traffic again.
On a copy of the database at production size, the whole rollback job was timed three times, taking 5, 6 and 6 minutes from its start to 7.2 serving traffic.

Repeats with one key are collapsed by the capture endpoint: in staging, 1,000 captures each submitted 6 times yielded exactly 1,000 charges, and the payments team has confirmed that behaviour as the endpoint's documented contract.
Each attempt, including every retry, generates a fresh random UUID and sends it as the idempotency key.
The two roots carry the same subject name and differ only in key identifier, and staging clients given a bundle with both accepted certificates issued by either one.
The cache key is "dash:{dashboard_id}:{range}", and the handler only ever reads or writes the key built from the current request.
The release also adds a nullable column 'split_payment_ref' to the orders table, which held a lock for under 1 second on a full-size staging copy and is not written while the flag is off.
The 14 existing callers have not been run against version 3.0; so far only the new refunds module has been exercised with it.
A nullable 'split_payment_ref' column is also added to the orders table; on a full-size staging copy it held a lock for under 1 second, and no writes reach it with the flag off.
Nobody has confirmed with the provider which limits actually apply to our account, and the plan contains no figure for them.
Its input is the closed month-end snapshot, which stays fixed after the month is closed, and the job splits it into batches of 500 records.
In flags.yaml the default is true for dev, true for staging and true for production.
Retention is 7 days for base backups and archived WAL alike, with anything past that age removed by a nightly lifecycle job.
On day 5 'Internal Root 2023' is removed from the trust bundle, and its private key, kept offline since day 1, is destroyed.
The two roots carry the same subject name and differ only in key identifier, and staging clients given a bundle with both accepted certificates issued by either one.
Nobody has tried writing to exports-prod/nightly/ with svc-export's own credentials, and what permissions it holds on that bucket has not been checked.
Keys take the form "dash:{dashboard_id}:{range}", and the handler touches no key other than the one derived from the request in hand.
Nobody has run a duplicate query on production, so whether rows created before release 4.9 contain duplicate (tenant_id, email) pairs is still unchecked.
On restock, the worker acquires reserve_mu first, takes stock_mu without releasing reserve_mu, adds the delivered units, prunes expired reservations, and then lets go of both.
Flag defaults in flags.yaml are true in dev, true in staging and true in production.
CI runs the checkout suite twice in staging, once with the flag on and once with it forced off to mirror production.
The job's throughput on a production-class host has not been measured, so how long 1.3 TB takes there is not known.

The rollback job has not been timed on a production-sized copy of the database, so how long the down-migration and redeploy take at 400 GB is not known.
Rollback is one pipeline job that starts automatically when the release is declared failed, runs the down-migration, and then redeploys version 7.2.
Under DEBUG, the logger adds each request header's name and value, substituting the string '[redacted]' for the values of Authorization, Cookie and X-Api-Key.
The restock worker locks reserve_mu, then locks stock_mu while still holding reserve_mu, adds the delivered units, trims expired reservations, and releases both.
None of the 14 existing callers has been executed on version 3.0 yet; the only code exercised with it so far is the new refunds module.
No write to exports-prod/nightly/ has been attempted with svc-export's own credentials, and its permissions on that bucket have not been checked.
The service account svc-export runs the export a single time at 01:00, and no retry follows a failed run.
No throughput figure has been measured for this job on a production-class machine, so the time a 1.3 TB night would take there is unknown.
Rows created before release 4.9 have not been checked for duplicate (tenant_id, email) pairs, and no duplicate query has been run on production.
